title: From address bar to rendered page
whole: A browser turns a typed URL into pixels through a pipeline: find the server, open a secure channel, exchange HTTP messages, then parse and paint.

source.title: From address bar to rendered page
source.text:
# What happens between typing an address and seeing the page

When you type `https://example.com/products?id=7` and press Enter, the browser has to turn a string into pixels. Nothing in that string says where the server is, how to talk to it, or how to draw its answer. The browser therefore runs a pipeline: it interprets the input, finds the server, opens a secure channel, asks for the document, and then parses and paints what comes back. Each stage depends on the previous one, and each has its own caches and failure modes.

## 1. Interpreting the input

The address bar is both a URL field and a search box. The browser first decides which one you meant. If the text parses as a URL with a known scheme, or looks like a host name, it is navigated to. Otherwise it is sent to the default search engine.

A URL is split into a scheme (`https`), a host (`example.com`), an optional port (default 443 for HTTPS, 80 for HTTP), a path (`/products`), a query (`?id=7`) and a fragment (`#section`). The fragment is never sent to the server; it is used only inside the browser after the page loads.

Before any network traffic, the browser checks local state:

- HSTS: if the host is on the browser's HSTS list (or was previously served a `Strict-Transport-Security` header), a typed `http://` is upgraded to `https://` internally, without a plain-text request.
- The HTTP cache: if a fresh copy of this URL is stored, according to its `Cache-Control` or `Expires` headers, the browser can skip the network entirely and go straight to rendering.
- Service workers: if a service worker is registered for this origin, it intercepts the request and may answer from its own cache or fetch from the network on its own terms.

If none of these answers the request, the browser needs a network connection to the server.

## 2. Finding the server: DNS

Networks route by IP address, not by name, so `example.com` must be turned into an address. This is DNS resolution, and it goes through layers of caches, from nearest to farthest:

1. The browser's own DNS cache.
2. The operating system's resolver cache, plus the local `hosts` file.
3. The configured recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP, your router or a public service. It has a large shared cache.
4. If the resolver has no answer, it walks the hierarchy: it asks a root server which servers handle `.com`, asks the `.com` servers which servers are authoritative for `example.com`, and asks those for the record.

The answer is an `A` record (IPv4) or `AAAA` record (IPv6), sometimes after following a `CNAME` alias. Each record carries a TTL that says how long every cache may reuse it. A short TTL lets operators move traffic quickly; a long TTL saves lookups. Modern browsers often ask for both `A` and `AAAA` and use a "happy eyeballs" strategy: they race IPv6 and IPv4 connections and keep the first that succeeds, so a broken IPv6 path does not stall the page.

Plain DNS runs over UDP port 53 and is unencrypted. DNS over HTTPS or DNS over TLS wraps the same questions in an encrypted channel so that other parties on the network cannot read which names you look up.

## 3. Opening a connection: TCP (or QUIC)

With an IP address, the browser opens a connection to port 443. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 this is TCP, which gives the application a reliable, ordered byte stream on top of an unreliable network. TCP starts with a three-way handshake:

- client → server: `SYN` (I want to connect, my sequence numbers start at X)
- server → client: `SYN-ACK` (accepted, mine start at Y)
- client → server: `ACK` (confirmed)

This costs one round trip before any data can flow. TCP then regulates its sending rate with congestion control: it starts small (slow start) and grows the window as acknowledgements arrive, so a fresh connection is slow for the first few round trips. That is one reason browsers reuse connections instead of opening new ones.

HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC, which runs over UDP. QUIC folds the transport and TLS handshakes together and moves the reliability logic into user space, so it needs fewer round trips and avoids one lost packet blocking unrelated streams. The browser learns that a server supports HTTP/3 from an `Alt-Svc` header or an HTTPS DNS record, and usually reaches it on a later visit.

## 4. Securing the connection: TLS

Because the scheme is `https`, the browser must establish an encrypted and authenticated channel before sending the request. In TLS 1.3 this takes one round trip:

1. The client sends `ClientHello`: the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, a random value, a key share for key exchange, and the server name in the SNI extension, so that a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to present. It also lists the application protocols it speaks (ALPN), such as `h2` and `http/1.1`.
2. The server replies with `ServerHello`, its own key share, its certificate chain, and a signature proving it holds the certificate's private key. It selects the protocol (ALPN).
3. Both sides derive the same session keys from the key exchange (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman). All later traffic is encrypted with them. Because the keys are ephemeral, recording today's traffic and stealing the server key later does not decrypt it (forward secrecy).

The browser validates the certificate chain. It checks that the chain leads to a certificate authority in its trust store, that the dates are valid, that the certificate has not been revoked (by OCSP stapling or browser-distributed revocation lists), and that the certificate's names include the host being visited. If any check fails, the browser shows a warning and stops. A resumed session can use a ticket from an earlier visit to skip part of this work, and with 0-RTT the client may even send the first request with its first flight, at the price of weaker replay protection.

## 5. Sending the request

Over the secure channel the browser sends an HTTP request. In HTTP/1.1 it is text:

```
GET /products?id=7 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: text/html
Accept-Encoding: gzip, br
Cookie: session=abc123
User-Agent: ...
```

The method and path say what is wanted; headers carry context. `Host` lets one IP address serve many sites. `Accept-Encoding` offers compression. `Cookie` returns any cookies the server previously set for this site, which is how stateless HTTP carries a login.

HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send the same information in a binary format. They compress headers (HPACK or QPACK) and multiplex many requests over one connection as independent streams. HTTP/1.1 can carry only one request at a time per connection, so browsers open several connections in parallel; HTTP/2 makes that unnecessary.

## 6. What the server does

The request reaches the server's network edge, which is often not the application itself. A typical path is a CDN or edge cache, then a load balancer, then a reverse proxy such as nginx, then the application. Any layer may answer from a cache. If the request goes all the way through, the application routes `/products` to a handler, authenticates the cookie, queries a database or other services, and builds a response, either an HTML document rendered on the server or a minimal shell that the browser will fill in with JavaScript.

The response has a status line, headers and a body:

```
HTTP/2 200
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Encoding: br
Cache-Control: max-age=60
Set-Cookie: ...

<!doctype html> ...
```

The status code tells the browser how to proceed. `200` means success. `301` or `302` with a `Location` header sends the browser back to step 1 for another URL. `304` means the cached copy is still valid. `4xx` and `5xx` are client and server errors. The `Content-Type` header tells the browser how to interpret the body, and `Content-Encoding` says it was compressed. `Cache-Control` tells the browser, and every cache in between, how long the response may be reused.

## 7. Turning bytes into a page: parsing

The browser receives the body in chunks and starts working before the whole document has arrived. This is called streaming parsing.

First the bytes are decoded to characters using the declared encoding. The HTML tokenizer then converts characters into tokens, and the tree builder turns tokens into the DOM, a tree of nodes in memory that mirrors the document structure. HTML parsing is deliberately forgiving: malformed markup is repaired by fixed rules rather than rejected.

While parsing, the browser finds further resources: stylesheets, scripts, images, fonts. A "preload scanner" runs ahead of the main parser to discover these early and start downloading them in parallel, each going through the same cache, DNS, connection and request steps above (usually reusing the existing connection).

Two kinds of resource interfere with parsing:

- CSS is render-blocking. The browser will not paint until it has the stylesheets, because painting without them would show unstyled content that then jumps. It parses CSS into the CSSOM, a tree of style rules.
- A plain `<script>` is parser-blocking. HTML parsing stops while the script is fetched and executed, because the script might change the document being built (for example with `document.write`) and it may also need the CSSOM to be ready first. The attributes `defer` (run after parsing, in order) and `async` (run as soon as downloaded, in any order) remove this blocking. Module scripts behave like `defer`.

## 8. From trees to pixels: rendering

The rendering pipeline combines the DOM and the CSSOM:

1. Style: for every DOM node, the browser computes the final style by resolving the cascade, specificity and inheritance. The result is a computed style for each element.
2. Layout: the browser computes the size and position of every box, following the box model, the flow of text and flexbox or grid rules. It produces a layout tree. Elements with `display: none` are absent from it.
3. Paint: for each box, the browser records drawing instructions: background, border, text, images, in the right stacking order.
4. Compositing: the page is divided into layers (for example elements with transforms, `position: fixed` or animations). Layers are rasterised into bitmaps, often on the GPU, and then composited in order to form the final frame on screen.

The first frame the user sees marks metrics such as First Contentful Paint. The biggest visible element's paint is the Largest Contentful Paint. Both depend directly on how quickly the earlier stages completed.

## 9. JavaScript and the event loop

JavaScript runs on the main thread, the same thread that does style, layout and most painting. That is why a long-running script freezes the page: while it runs, the browser cannot respond to clicks or draw a new frame. The event loop alternates between running one task (a script, an event handler, a timer callback), running all pending microtasks (promise callbacks), and, when it is time, rendering a frame.

Scripts can change the DOM or the styles at any moment. Each change marks part of the pipeline as invalid. The browser batches these, then re-runs style, layout and paint only for what changed at the next frame. Reading layout values such as `offsetHeight` right after writing styles forces the browser to compute layout immediately (a forced synchronous layout); alternating reads and writes in a loop, called layout thrashing, is a common cause of slowness.

In a client-rendered application, the first HTML is nearly empty. The page appears only after the script bundle has been downloaded, parsed and executed, and after it has fetched its data (for example with `fetch`) and built the DOM. Server-side rendering and static generation move that work to the server so that the first response already contains content; the script then attaches behaviour to the existing markup (hydration).

## 10. Everything else that finishes the page

The page is not complete when the first frame appears. Images and fonts continue to arrive; the browser may swap in a web font after first showing a fallback. The `load` event fires when the document and its sub-resources are done. Later requests from scripts can keep the connection busy. Cookies set by responses are stored for the next request. Response headers such as `Cache-Control` decide what the next visit can skip, which is why a repeat visit is much faster: DNS, the connection and many resources may all come from cache.

## Where time goes

Following one navigation, the main costs appear in order:

- DNS lookup: usually one round trip to a resolver, zero if cached.
- TCP handshake: one round trip.
- TLS handshake: one round trip with TLS 1.3 (two with TLS 1.2).
- Request and first byte (time to first byte): one round trip plus the server's processing time.
- Download, parse, fetch sub-resources, render: bandwidth, CPU and the number of dependent requests.

Because several of these are round trips, latency (distance and network quality) often matters more than raw bandwidth. This explains the common optimisations: CDNs put the server closer, connection reuse and HTTP/3 remove handshakes, compression and caching shrink or remove transfers, `defer` and preloading unblock parsing, and server-side rendering shortens the path to the first meaningful paint.

traces.question: What happens after I type a URL and press Enter?

steps.text: The browser reads the input and tries HSTS, cache and service workers
DNS turns the host name into an IP address
A TCP (or QUIC) connection is opened to port 443
TLS authenticates the server and derives session keys
The HTTP request is sent over the secure channel
Edge layers or the application build the response, whose status and headers steer the browser
The body is parsed into the DOM, with CSS and scripts discovered on the way
Style, layout, paint and compositing produce the frame
